title: Wycliffe's Bible
hookLine: an Oxford scholar and his followers translate the Bible into English, against the law

cards: Set the scene this way. A man stands at the edge of a field in England, leaning on his plough, while someone reads to him from a small handwritten book.

The words are the Gospels, and this time he understands them, because they're in English. In his parish church the readings come in Latin, the language of scholars and priests. He has heard about the Bible all his life.
Now he's hearing it. Behind that little book stands an Oxford scholar named John Wycliffe, and the followers who carried his work on.

teach.b: John Wycliffe taught at Oxford, and grew convinced of something that sounds simple and was explosive: ordinary Christians should be able to read the scriptures for themselves, in their own language.
He criticized the church's wealth and argued that scripture should judge the church, not the other way around. His followers, sometimes called Lollards, set out to put the whole Bible into English.

teach.h: COPIED BY HAND, FROM THE LATIN.
teach.b: They worked from the church's Latin Bible, and every copy was written by hand, because printing hadn't come to England yet. Copies spread among townspeople and country folk.
Church authorities in England saw danger in it: errors, divisions, unrest.
Before long, making or owning a new English translation without a bishop's approval was forbidden, and some caught with these books were punished. Christians still weigh that history differently.
Some see the church protecting people from mistakes; others see it keeping the word from them. But the hope behind the work is very old.

teach.h: EVERY MAN IN OUR OWN TONGUE.
teach.b: At Pentecost, in Acts, a crowd from many nations hears the apostles, and the King James Bible gives their astonished question: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

That's this week's thread too: Sergius sharing bread at the forest's edge, Rublev leaving a place open, priests who stayed with the sick, Julian at her window, Catherine writing to the pope, Bridget beginning again as a widow.
Faith brought out onto ordinary ground. Wycliffe's followers brought the book itself.

how: Christians today read the Bible in their own languages, at home and aloud in worship, and Wycliffe's translation is remembered as part of the long story of putting scripture into ordinary speech.

games.q: you're a scholar who believes ordinary people should read the Bible in their own language, but the church reads it in Latin. what do you do?
o: keep it in Latin and explain it in sermons.
put it into English, and let copies spread.
wait for church leaders to approve first.
games.why: Wycliffe's followers put the whole Bible into English, and handwritten copies spread among ordinary people.

practice: Pick one short passage, the opening of John's Gospel or a psalm if you don't know where to start, and read it once quietly.
Then read it again, aloud if you can, letting each word land as if you'd never heard it in your own language before, the way that ploughman did.
If you pray, let the words become your prayer; if not, stay with whichever word stops you.

wordCard.voice: Wycliffe's Bible. The handwritten English Bible made by John Wycliffe's followers from the Latin, so ordinary people could hear scripture in their own tongue.
